options.explanation: Absolute zero sits 273 degrees below the freezing point of water.

questions.stem: Why is a temperature below absolute zero impossible?

options.text: the Celsius scale simply ends there
options.explanation: Scales are conventions; the limit is physical.

options.text: particle motion is already at its minimum there and cannot be reduced further
options.explanation: Coldness is slowed particles; there is no slower-than-minimum state.

options.text: thermometers stop working below that point
options.explanation: Instrument limits are not nature's limits.

options.text: all gases have frozen solid long before
options.explanation: Some substances are still fluid near absolute zero; the limit is deeper than freezing.

questions.stem: What happens to the pressure of an ideal fixed-volume gas as its temperature approaches absolute zero?

options.explanation: Pressure tracks temperature at fixed volume.
A gas cannot pull on the walls; pressure bottoms at zero.

options.text: it falls towards zero because the wall collisions die away
options.explanation: No motion means no collisions and no pressure.
Cooling lowers pressure; heating raises it.

options.text: gas thermometers are all broken the same way

options.text: absolute zero is a universal property of temperature, not of any one gas

options.text: the molecules would have minimum kinetic energy, so wall collisions cease
options.explanation: Pressure is wall bombardment; still molecules deliver none.

options.text: the molecules would sink to the bottom

Containers do not grow at low temperature.

questions.stem: State the temperature of absolute zero.
questions.modelAnswer: Absolute zero is −273 °C, the lowest temperature possible.

questions.stem: State what happens to the kinetic energy of particles as a substance is cooled towards absolute zero.
questions.modelAnswer: The kinetic energy of the particles falls towards the minimum possible value as their motion slows.

questions.stem: Explain how a pressure–temperature graph provides evidence for a lowest possible temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: For a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, pressure falls linearly as temperature falls. Extrapolating the straight line beyond the measured range, the pressure reaches zero at −273 °C for every gas tried. A gas cannot exert less than zero pressure, so temperature cannot continue below the point where the bombardment vanishes — the graph therefore exposes a hard floor for temperature itself.

questions.stem: A fixed-volume gas thermometer reads 0 Pa of gas pressure in an ideal extrapolation. State the corresponding temperature in °C and in kelvin.
questions.modelAnswer: Zero ideal-gas pressure corresponds to absolute zero: −273 °C, which is 0 K on the Kelvin scale.

questions.stem: Why do gas-law calculations require kelvin rather than Celsius?

options.text: kelvin numbers are larger and easier
options.explanation: Convenience is not the reason; correctness is.
The physics, not the preference, demands kelvin.

options.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature, linearly.

options.text: it doubles; the Celsius pair is −123 °C to 27 °C
options.explanation: 150 K = −123 °C and 300 K = 27 °C; kelvin doubles energy.

questions.stem: State the conversion from kelvin to degrees Celsius.
questions.modelAnswer: Subtract 273 from the kelvin temperature to get the temperature in degrees Celsius.

questions.stem: State the temperature of absolute zero in kelvin and in degrees Celsius.
questions.modelAnswer: Absolute zero is 0 K, which equals −273 °C on the Celsius scale.

questions.stem: Explain why saying '27 °C is twice as hot as 13.5 °C' is meaningless while '300 K is twice 150 K' is meaningful.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature ratios are only physical when measured from the true zero of energy, which is 0 K. Celsius's zero is an arbitrary water-based mark 273 degrees above that floor, so its ratios compare offsets from an arbitrary line. Kelvin starts where molecular energy starts, so doubling kelvin genuinely doubles the mean kinetic energy of the molecules.

questions.stem: A gas law problem gives the initial temperature as 20 °C and requires doubling the kelvin temperature. Calculate the target temperature in °C.
questions.modelAnswer: 20 °C = 293 K. Doubling gives 586 K, and converting back: 586 − 273 = 313 °C. Note the answer is not 40 °C — Celsius ratios are not physical.
